beats.text: London, seventeen sixty-three. The person you love lives in Edinburgh. And you want to see them.
The coach takes two weeks. And it only leaves once a month.
Four hundred miles of muddy roads. The horses are changed again and again. Every night, you stop at an inn.
In seventeen eighty-four, John Palmer had an idea. Put the mail on fast coaches. Fresh horses every few miles. And a guard with a gun.
But by eighteen thirty, mail coaches ran day and night. London to Edinburgh, in under two days.
So in seventy years, two weeks shrank to two days.
Then came the railway. The telegraph. And the phone.
Today, your message arrives before you put the phone down.
Two weeks, to see the one you love. Two seconds, to tell them.

sources: 1763: one stage coach a month from Edinburgh to London, 12–14 days; about 1830: six or seven coaches a day, about 48 hours. All the Year Round (Dickens' magazine), vol. VI, p. 302. 1829: the North Mail London→Edinburgh in about 43.5 hours. The Spectator, 11 July 1829, 'The North Mail'.

The lovers are illustrative. London–Edinburgh ≈ 400 miles by road; overnight stops at inns on 18th-century stage-coach journeys. Film: 'Fast Mail, Northern Pacific R.R.' (Edison, 1897), public domain, illustrative (Internet Archive).
John Palmer's mail coaches from 1784 (first run Bristol–London), horses changed at stages, armed Royal Mail guard: Postal Museum (UK), 'Mail coaches'.
